title: Backcasting approach with multi-scenario simulation for assessing effects of land use policy using GeoSOS-FLUS software
author: Wang, Shen, et al.

steps.title: Define initial and target scenarios
steps.instruction: Set the initial land‑use scenario to the Su‑Jia‑Hu area in the year 2000 and the target scenario to the same area in 2015. Using the ArcGIS property table, calculate the area (km²) of each land‑use type for 2000 and 2015 and record them in a table (e.g., Forest 2750.79 → 2695.16, Pasture 101.03 → 100.82, River 633.68 → 608.71, Lake and pond 2737.29 → 3042.88, Wetland 99.33 → 101.36, Unused land 7.44 → 12.69, Cultivated land 10112.79 → 7705.93, City and town 572.10 → 1603.23, Rural residential 1227.68 → 1458.70, Transport 92.84 → 233.91, Industrial 145.04 → 778.12, Other construction 55.90 → 194.40).

steps.title: Collect land‑use policies
steps.instruction: Search official websites of the three cities in Su‑Jia‑Hu, Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, the environmental conservation bureau, the land‑resources bureau and government bulletins for land‑use policies issued between 1995 and 2015. Identify 46 policies that directly or indirectly affect land‑use change; 37 affect conversion between natural and unnatural spaces, 4 affect conversion within natural spaces, and 16 affect conversion within unnatural spaces.

steps.title: Classify policies and land‑use types
steps.instruction: Divide land‑use types into natural spaces (forest, pasture, river, lake & pond, wetland, unused land) and unnatural spaces (cultivated land, city & town, rural residential, transport, industrial, other construction). Classify each policy into three conversion categories: (i) between natural and unnatural spaces, (ii) within natural spaces, (iii) within unnatural spaces (mainly construction ↔ cultivated land).

steps.title: Grade policy intensity and direction
steps.instruction: Label each policy with intensity: Direct (D), Indirect (I), Strong (S), Weak (W). Label direction as Positive (+) or Negative (−). Compute the assignment Q for each policy using Q = P × M, where P = 9 for D‑S, 5 for D‑W or I‑S, 1 for I‑W; M = +1 for “+”, –1 for “−”.

steps.title: Number policies and build cost matrix
steps.instruction: Assign each policy a code “policy‑number‑intensity‑direction”. Using the 46 coded policies, construct the land‑use conversion cost matrix. For each cell (i → j), calculate Value = Σ_{k∈nij} Q_k. If the minimum Value across the matrix (minValue) is ≥0, set V = Value; if minValue < 0, set V = Value + minValue. Interpret V = 0 as prohibited conversion, V = 1 as fully encouraged, and 0 < V < 1 as intermediate cost.

steps.title: Compute land‑use expansion coefficients
steps.instruction: For each land‑use type u, calculate the average annual growth rate Ru = (Au2015 – Au2000) / Au2000 × 15 × 100 %. If minRate_u ≥ 0, set Ru = Rate_u; otherwise Ru = Rate_u + minRate_u. Then compute the expansion coefficient Wu = Ru_max / Ru.

steps.title: Run initial GeoSOS‑FLUS simulation
steps.instruction: Input the initial conversion cost matrix and expansion coefficients into GeoSOS‑FLUS. Generate the 2015 simulated land‑use map. Extract simulated areas for each land‑use type and calculate systematic error = (Simulated – Actual) / Actual × 100 %. Compare these errors with the ±5 % accuracy threshold (Table 2). Note that several types (e.g., Unused land –43.41 %, Transport –60.28 %) exceed the threshold.

steps.title: Iteratively adjust cost matrix
steps.instruction: Apply the following rules to each i → j conversion: (1) If simulated area of i > actual and simulated area of j < actual, increase the cost parameter for i → j; (2) If simulated i < actual and simulated j > actual, decrease the cost parameter for i → j; (3) Otherwise leave unchanged. Re‑run the simulation after each adjustment, recalculate systematic errors, and repeat until all land‑use types have systematic error within ±5 %. In this study five adjustment rounds were performed, after which errors fell within the range (see Table 3).

steps.title: Generate final simulation results
steps.instruction: After the fifth adjustment, produce the final simulated 2015 land‑use map and record the areas (e.g., Forest 2695.16 → 730.82, Pasture 100.82 → 101.03, River 608.71 → 630.70, etc.). Verify that systematic errors for all types except Unused land and Transport are within ±5 % (Unused land error –43.41 % is ignored due to its small absolute area; Transport error –60.28 % is ignored because transport occupies only 1.26 % of total area).

steps.title: Translate parameters back to policies
steps.instruction: For each cell of the final conversion cost matrix, reduce the value to the set of policy numbers nij that generated it (as in formula 4). Classify each nij as “Up regulation”, “Down regulation”, or “Without changes”. The “Without changes” set represents effective policies; the other two sets represent failure policies.

steps.title: Analyze policy effectiveness and failure
steps.instruction: Compare the initial and final parameter matrices (Tables S2 and S4). Map the policy numbers to intensity/direction and grade them (Tables S5, S6). Categorize effective policies into: A – direct natural‑space protection, B – non‑mandatory restrictions on natural‑to‑unnatural conversion, C – legal basis for natural‑to‑unnatural conversion, D – direct cultivated‑land protection. Classify failure policies as spatial‑structure failure or total‑quantity failure, and further grade the latter as low, medium, or high degree based on the magnitude of parameter adjustment. Discuss qualitative reasons for each failure (e.g., inefficient, excessive, absent policies). Produce the final lists of effective and failure policies.

description: This stage is the last two steps of applying this method to assess the effects of land use policies. Firstly, contrast the initial parameter combination and the parameter combination of final scenario simulation in Tables S2 and S4. For the same part of the parameters that can reflect the evolution characteristics and rules of land-use/cover in this period under specific constraint conditions or action mechanisms, translate them back into policy numbers and explain the effectiveness of land use policies on natural spaces changing. For the different part of the parameters which show the ineffectiveness of land-use/cover mechanism, after translating back to the policies they represent, it is necessary to analyze possible failure causes of these land use policies. The conversion cost parameters in Tables S2 and S4 are translated into the land use policy numbers as follows: first, the values in each cell in the initial conversion cost matrix (Table S2) are reduced to the policy number set for converting i -type land to j -type land, namely nij in formula (4). Secondly, the nij in each cell is corresponding to the parameter adjustment type in the scenario simulation conversion cost matrix (Table S4). The nij corresponding to the class "Up regulation" or "Down regulation" represents the invalidation policy number set, and the nij corresponding to the class "Without changes" represents the effective policy number set. After translating the parameter values into the corresponding policy action mechanism numbers (“policy number” and “policy intensity and direction”), the land use policies are classified and graded (see Tables S5 and S6 in Supplementary material), which reflect the effect and intensity of the land use policies on land use changes in Su-Jia-Hu Area from 2000 to 2015.
